newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico hopes to put peace talks back on track.
newsitem.headline: Mexico hopes to put peace talks back on track.

text.p: The Mexican government and Zapatista rebels have reached an impasse in peace talks but a government peace negotiator held out hope on Monday that the two sides could get back together.

"The dialogue is not broken," said a member of Cocopa, the government negotiating commission, who asked not to be identified because the panel was to make an official pronouncement on the talks on Tuesday.

The peace process in southeastern Chiapas state reached perhaps its lowest ebb this weekend when Zapatista leader Subcommander Marcos condemned a government proposal on Indian rights, calling it "racist, ethnocentric and discriminatory."
The guerrillas then retreated to the Chiapas jungle, where they are surrounded by the army as a ceasefire holds.

The Zapatistas and Cocopa reached an accord on Indian rights last year after months of negotiations, but the language was changed by the government and Congress in a bid to convert the agreement into constitutional amendments.

When the revised document reached the Zapatistas in their jungle hideaway, the predominantly Maya Indian fighters rejected it. Marcos, the charismatic non-Indian leader known by his ski mask and pipe, declared the peace process "in crisis" at a weekend news conference in Chiapas.

The government responded immediately, placing the blame on the Zapatistas for rejecting an accord that would grant Indian communities autonomy, preserve their customs, allow them to choose their own leaders and grant them special access to natural resources.

The agreeement on Indian rights was long thought to have been a settled issue and the two sides had gone to work on a more difficult accord on reforming the Mexican political system. Those talks broke down four months ago.

On Jan. 1, 1994, the Zapatista guerrillas launched their uprising in Chiapas after training in the jungle for years. After 11 days of combat in which an estimated 145 people were killed, the government declared a unilateral ceasefire. The two sides sat down to start peace talks in April 1995.
